meta.title: Building a Search Engine From Scratch, Part 1: The Inverted Index
meta.excerpt: How do you find a needle in 50,000 haystacks in a few milliseconds? You stop searching the haystacks and start searching a map of where the needles are.
meta.author: Williams Adusei

Building a Search Engine From Scratch  Part 1: The Inverted Index

I'm fascinated by how search engines like Google and Bing work under the hood but the information on the internet on how to implement one yourself is fragmented,we'll build one from scratch without any huge libraries. Reach out if you need any help, I'd be glad to help 😊

1. A Short History of Finding Things

Every day, billions of people type a few words into a box and, in well under a second, get back a ranked list of relevant pages pulled from an index of an almost incomprehensible size. It feels like magic. It isn't. It is a handful of beautifully simple ideas, refined over decades, stacked on top of each other. This series is about rebuilding those ideas ourselves, one layer at a time.
But before we write a single line of logic, it is worth knowing where those ideas came from.
The first tool widely recognised as an Internet search engine was
in Montreal (with Bill Heelan and Peter Deutsch). Archie predates the World Wide Web. It periodically downloaded the file listings of public FTP servers and let you search those
. It did not know what was
the files  only what they were called. Still, the core idea was already there:
do the expensive work of collecting information ahead of time, so that answering a question later is cheap.
The Early Web: Directories and Crawlers (1994-1996)
When the Web exploded in the mid-1990s, two very different approaches emerged:
Yahoo! (1994, started by Stanford students Jerry Yang and David Filo)
People manually categorised websites into a hierarchy
Could not keep up with the growth of the Web
Software "spiders" downloaded pages and indexed every word
Full-text engines like AltaVista were technically impressive  they could tell you

2. Life After Google: Lucene, Elasticsearch and Algolia

Web search is the most visible kind of search, but it's far from the only one. Every time you search your email, filter products on an e-commerce site, look up a log line in a monitoring dashboard, or hit
on a documentation site, a search engine is running. Most of those search engines don't crawl the Web  they index a company's
data. But underneath, they play the same game.
who had previously worked on search at Xerox PARC, Apple and Excite  wrote
in Java, and released it as open source. (The name is his wife's middle name.) Lucene joined the
in 2001 and became a top-level Apache project in 2005. Cutting would later go on to co-create
Lucene is not a server or a product  it's the engine block. At its heart is, unsurprisingly, an inverted index, stored in immutable files called
that are periodically merged together. Lucene powers an astonishing amount of the world's search, mostly indirectly, through the systems built on top of it:

started playing with an early version of Lucene while living in London, building a recipe search engine for his wife, who was attending culinary school. That experiment grew into an open-source project called
, which made Lucene easier to use from Java applications. Realising that the world needed something distributed and scalable, he rewrote it from scratch, and in
: Lucene wrapped in a distributed server, spoken to over HTTP with JSON. Its company, now
, built the well-known "ELK" stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana). Every shard of an Elasticsearch cluster is  you guessed it  a Lucene index, which is an inverted index.
was founded in 2012 in Paris by
offline search engine SDK for mobile apps
, where speed and tiny memory footprints were non-negotiable. The market for offline mobile search proved small, so  around the time they went through
(Winter 2014 batch)  they pivoted to a hosted

, bringing that obsession with speed and instant "search-as-you-type" relevance to websites and apps. Different business, different engine (they built their own rather than using Lucene), same foundational idea.
Fifty years of progress in ranking, distribution, typo-tolerance and machine learning  and the inverted index is still there, quietly doing the heavy lifting. That's what we're going to build today.
3. What We Are Building in This Series
By the end of this series you'll have built a working search engine from first principles. No search libraries, no databases, no magic.
A few ground rules for how this series is written:
Our reference implementation is in Python, but this post contains
. Instead, we explain every step in terms of
data structures, algorithms and a bit of maths
, so you can implement it in Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, C#, Rust, C++  whatever you're comfortable with.
If you've never heard of a hash map, that's fine. We'll explain every structure as we meet it.
We're here to understand how a search engine
. We'll keep document parsing deliberately simple for now and give it the attention it deserves in a later post.
4. The Problem: Why Not Just Scan Everything?
Our dataset is a single text file of about
The most obvious approach is: open the file, read every article from top to bottom, and collect the ones that contain the word "quantum". This is called a
, and it's what a "find" feature in a text editor does.
It works. It's also terrible for a search engine:
Look up one entry, read a short list
Think about a printed textbook. If you want to find every page that mentions "photosynthesis", you don't read the book cover to cover. You flip to the
, find "photosynthesis  pages 45, 112, 230", and go straight there.
, when the book was printed, so that every reader could find things
. That's precisely the trade an inverted index makes:
Spend a lot of time and memory up-front (indexing) so that every future question (query) is cheap.

Today our parsing is intentionally minimal, so we can focus on the engine.

We use one simple, precise rule:
A token is any unbroken run of the characters `a``z` and `0``9`. Any other character (space, punctuation, hyphen, bracket, symbol, accented letter...) acts as a separator.
In regular-expression notation, this rule is written

(If you'd rather not use regular expressions, you can implement the same rule by walking through the string one character at a time: keep appending characters to the current token while they're alphanumeric, and "close" the token whenever you hit any other character.)

Tokenisation is a surprisingly deep rabbit hole (think URLs, email addresses, "C++", "U.S.A.", Chinese text with no spaces at all...), and production engines like Lucene ship with many configurable tokenisers. For learning the core of a search engine, a simple rule applied consistently beats a clever rule applied inconsistently.
Some words are everywhere. "the", "of", "and", "is", "to" appear in virtually every English document. A list of documents containing "the" is essentially a list of
documents  it tells us nothing useful, and it would be by far the largest entry in our index.
This is not a coincidence; it's a well-known statistical property of language called

: in a large body of text, a word's frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its rank. The most common word appears about twice as often as the second most common, three times as often as the third, and so on. A tiny number of words account for a huge fraction of all the text.

16. The Mathematics of an Inverted Index
You don't need maths to build an index, but describing it formally makes the design crystal clear, and the quantities we define here are the building blocks of ranking later in the series.
$D = \{d_0, d_1, \dots, d_{N-1}\}$ be the collection of $N$ documents, where each $d_j$ is identified by the integer $j$.
Each document, after the pipeline (tokenise → remove stop words → stem), becomes a
: $d_j = (t_{j,0},\ t_{j,1},\ \dots,\ t_{j,L_j - 1})$, where $L_j$ is the number of kept terms in document $j$.

Then the positional inverted index is a
that maps every term to its occurrences:
In words: "the positions $p$ in document $j$ where the term at position $p$ is $t$". The postings list for $t$ contains one entry for every document where that set is not empty.

How many times term $t$ appears in doc $j$ (length of the positions list)
How many documents contain $t$ (length of the postings list)
Total occurrences of $t$ in the whole corpus
Number of kept terms in document $j$

(low $df$) is a strong signal of what that document is about. That intuition is the basis of classic relevance scoring, and our index already contains everything needed to compute it.

20. Engineering Notes, Trade-offs and Known Limitations
Our indexer is deliberately simple, so it's honest to point out where a production system would do things differently. None of these matter for learning, but all of them matter at scale.
Build the index in memory-bounded chunks, flush each chunk to disk, then merge them (algorithms known as
). Lucene's segment model is a version of this idea
Write new documents into new small segments and merge segments in the background
Index on many cores and many machines, then combine
One tokeniser, 40 stop words, one stemmer, English only
Configurable analysers per field and per language
Look at a positions list like
. Instead of storing each position, we could store the first one as-is and then only the

. The same trick works for docIds in postings lists. Because lists are sorted (thank you, invariants!), gaps are always positive and usually small, and small numbers can be stored in fewer bytes using
. This is how real engines shrink positional indexes dramatically. Notice how sortedness, which we got for free in Step 7, keeps paying dividends.
A word in the title is treated exactly like a word in the body. In a real engine, a match in the title is usually a much stronger signal, so fields are indexed separately.

That's a parsing concern, and it's exactly why parsing gets its own post later in this series. (The two other parsing pitfalls we hit, Wikipedia IDs leaking into the text and the ghost empty document created by splitting, are already handled in Step 1.)
